item.title: Ask Ethan: Can you explain the Higgs boson in depth?
item.description:
One of the great quests in all of science is to discover, at a fundamental level, what the Universe is actually made of. If you took every amount of matter and energy that existed — or even could exist — and cut it up into its smallest possible chunks, until only something that was uncuttable was left, you’d be left with the fundamental, elementary particles that composed our Universe. In physics, this took us first down to the level of the atom, then to atomic nuclei and electrons, then to protons, neutrons, and electrons, and finally to our modern Standard Model of elementary particles: complete with quarks, charged leptons, neutrinos, their antimatter counterparts, the gluons, the photon, the W-and-Z bosons, and one additional unique particle, the Higgs boson.

Of all of those particles, the Higgs boson is the most recently discovered particle: found only at particle accelerators, like the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, in 2012. But what’s the story of the Higgs boson? What makes it so unique, where does it come from, and how does it fit in with everything else that we know? That’s what Vu H Nguyen wants to know, asking:

“Can you explain the Higgs boson in depth? [It is] difficult for me to understand, but I think this is very important in particle physics. Maybe you can explain it in an easier way?”

When we think about matter, we normally think about “fundamental” in the way we outlined above: by cutting it up into its smallest indivisible component parts. But there’s more to the story, and the Higgs boson requires us to go deeper than any other known particle in order to understand it. Here’s the story.

Here in our Universe, we’re mostly familiar with the particles that are common and stable today: atoms and the subatomic particles they’re composed of. Atoms are made of electrons that orbit the atomic nucleus, which in turn is made of protons and neutrons, which themselves are made of quarks and gluons.

If you want to see what types of quarks are in there, however, you have to collide particles together. You have to collide them hard enough to break inside the atom, to crack open the atomic nucleus, to split apart the individual protons and neutrons, and to smash them directly into individual elementary particles.

When you do that, you discover something amazing. You don’t just reveal what these composite structures inside the atom are made of; you also gain the ability to create brand new particles, including heavy, unstable, short-lived particles. Through the power of colliders, we don’t just make electrons and the up-and-down quarks that compose protons and neutrons, but also:

  • muons and taus, the heavier cousins of electrons,
  • positrons, antimuons, and antitaus, the antimatter counterparts of those charged leptons,
  • strange, charm, bottom, and top quarks,
  • the antimatter counterparts of all six flavors of quarks (the antiquarks),
  • photons, gluons, and W-and-Z bosons, which are the gauge bosons,
  • and the Higgs boson as well.

These, along with the neutrinos and antineutrinos (which can’t be directly observed in colliders, but can be observed through other means), make up all of the known elementary particles, and the entirety of the Standard Model of elementary particles.

We can measure all sorts of properties about these particles from our collider-detector experiments. In particular, we can, by creating enough of them and building detectors around the collision points where those particles come into existence — created from energy via Einstein’s E = mc as long as all of the necessary quantum properties like energy, momentum, angular momentum, electric charge, and so on are conserved — measure all sorts of properties associated with them. We can determine:

  • their rest masses,
  • their electric charges,
  • their intrinsic angular momenta (i.e., their spin),
  • their mean lifetimes,
  • their weak hypercharge and weak isospin,
  • their possible decay products (all of the different pathways through which the unstable ones can decay),
  • and their branching ratios (the rate at which they decay through their various pathways),

chief among them. The Standard Model isn’t just about the particles that exist, but about their key relationships and properties. The quarks and leptons make up what we conventionally know of as “matter” (while the antiquarks and antileptons make up “antimatter”), but the gauge bosons determine how they interact with one another. We normally talk about this as the four fundamental forces, as particles and antiparticles interact through gravity (which we don’t know whether it’s quantum in nature; it’s outside of the Standard Model), electromagnetism (mediated by the photon), the weak nuclear force (mediated by the W-and-Z bosons), and the strong nuclear force (mediated by the gluons).

Sure, there are still mysteries that we have that the Standard Model can’t explain: gravity, the values for the rest masses of the particles, the abundance of matter over antimatter in the Universe, and the existence of dark matter and dark energy among them. But for what the Standard Model does give us, it’s an incredibly powerful description of reality.

So where does the Higgs boson come from?

In order to answer that, we can’t start here in our Universe today, nor can we even start with the “little bangs” we create in our particle colliders here on Earth. Instead, we have to go all the way back to the hot Big Bang, where higher energies and hotter temperatures were achieved than in anything we can create here on Earth.

Back then, we still had the quarks and leptons (and antiquarks and antileptons) that we have today, as well as the gluons. They all still needed energy in order to exist, but they didn’t possess the rest masses that they have today. (You might have heard the phrase “the Higgs gives mass to the Universe,” but that refers to the Higgs field being “switched on” as opposed to “switched off,” not the Higgs boson!) Still, the particles existed just as they do today; that much was the same.

However, the other bosons looked very, very different. We didn’t have the photon, the W-and-Z bosons and the Higgs boson at all back in the early stages of the hot Big Bang. Instead, we had four massless bosons: the W1, W2, W3, and the B. The Higgs field was also there, but in a very different state to how it exists today. Whereas today, the Higgs field is in what’s known as a state of “broken symmetry,” like a ball that’s rolled down into a valley along the brim of a hat, early on, the Higgs field was in a “restored symmetry” state: like being at the top of the peak of the hat, where all directions appear equivalent.

What this means, at the high energies associated with the early stages of the hot Big Bang, is that there are the same spectrum of Standard Model fermions (quarks and leptons, and antiquarks and antileptons) that we have today, albeit without rest masses, but a different spectrum of forces that they interact through.

They interact through:

  • gravity (which isn’t included in the Standard Model),
  • the strong nuclear force (which is still mediated by the gluons back then, as it is today),
  • by the electroweak force (which is mediated by those W1, W2, W3, and B bosons, instead of today’s W-and-Z bosons and photon which mediate the weak nuclear and electromagnetic forces),
  • and through the Higgs field, which has four degrees of freedom in the same fashion that the electroweak force has four bosons associated with it).

According to the Standard Model, the Higgs field isn’t a vector field or a spinor field (like the other bosons and fermions), but rather is a scalar field. (In technical language, we call the structure of this field a complex SU(2) doublet.) At this point, there is still a Higgs field and a Higgs interaction, but no Higgs boson. In addition, the Standard Model particles haven’t yet acquired a rest mass.

And then, a critical transition happens: the Universe cools through an energy-equivalent of about 250 GeV, which happens about a picosecond (0.000000000001 seconds) after the start of the hot Big Bang. This is known as the electroweak phase transition: where the Higgs mechanism spontaneously breaks the unified electroweak force down into the separate electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces.

You’ll sometimes hear the terms “electroweak symmetry breaking” and “Higgs symmetry breaking” as though they are separate things; they are not. They are one and the same: the Higgs mechanism is the cause of electroweak symmetry breaking, and it occurs when the energy of the Universe drops significantly that it’s no longer energetically favorable to be on the “peak” of the hat-like potential. When you fall off of the peak and down towards the brim, that’s where it all occurs, and that’s ultimately the origin of the Higgs boson.

But before we get there, you have to understand there’s a theorem in physics known as Goldstone’s theorem that states that every time you have a continuous symmetry that’s spontaneously broken, you get a new massless scalar particle out of it: a particle known as a Nambu-Goldstone boson.

Because the Higgs field has a specific structure — that of a complex SU(2) doublet — that means it has four degrees of freedom with it, and hence, in its unbroken state, four continuous symmetries to it. When symmetry breaking occurs, we get, by Goldstone’s theorem, four massless scalar particles out of it.

But hang on! Doesn’t the Higgs boson have mass?

This is why it’s so important that we understand how the Higgs mechanism works. When those four continuous degrees of freedom all have their symmetry broken, four theoretically massless scalar, Higgs-related particles emerge:

  • a positively charged one, H+,
  • a negatively charged one, H–,
  • and two electrically neutral ones, normally called H0 and h.

But these are not isolated massless particles; they exist amidst the rest of the Universe. And here in this Universe, we also had those electroweak bosons: the W1, W2, W3, and B bosons.

Now, there’s one more piece of information we have that we need to put together. In our quantum Universe, if two distinct quantum particles have the same quantum numbers, they inevitably wind up having their wavefunctions overlap, and they mix together. With the new arrival of the H+, H–, H0 and h particles, the W1, W2, W3, and B bosons now have something to mix with.

The W1 and W2 particles already have the same quantum numbers, so they already mix together. (The W3 and B bosons also mix together, and that will be important in a bit.) One combination of the W1 and W2 then combines with the positively charged Higgs boson, H+, and creates the positively charged W-boson, W+. The other combination of W1 and W2 combines with the negatively charged Higgs boson, H–, to make the negatively charged W-boson, W–. These combinations, as gauge symmetries, now become massive.

There are also going to be two combinations of the W3 and B bosons, in similar fashion. One of those combinations combines with one of the neutral Higgs-related particles: H0. That combination becomes the neutral weak boson: Z0. The other combination of the W3 and B, however, doesn’t combine with, absorb, or eat anything; it remains massless, and that’s what becomes the photon. (If you’re asking, “hey, does that mean that prior to electroweak symmetry breaking, the Universe didn’t have photons in it?” The answer is yes!!)

That just leaves one degree of freedom left, h, with nothing to combine or mix with. That’s what becomes the massive Higgs boson.

But why does it become massive? Take a look, above, at the hat-like potential associated with the Higgs field. Three of those degrees of freedom of the field represent what’s called the azimuthal direction of the field: the components of the field that go around, either clockwise or counterclockwise, of the “brim” of that hat within the valley. (More technically, they correspond to the positive, negative, and neutral currents in that azimuthal direction.) That’s what combines with the three of the initial electroweak gauge bosons to make the W-and-Z bosons, with the last uncombined electroweak gauge boson making the massless photon.

However, that last degree of freedom — the one associated with h — moves in the radial direction instead: the one that fights to go up-and-down towards or away from the hat’s center. Unlike the “around” going (azimuthal) direction, which is flat and uncurved, the radial direction is heavily curved. If you think of that component of the field as a ball, it’s going to roll up-and-down the sides of that hat, and therefore will oscillate. Those oscillations is how that component of the field acquires a mass, and is why the Higgs boson, the particle associated with h, turns out to be massive.

It’s the coupling to the Higgs field that gives the massive Standard Model particles their non-zero rest masses, but it’s a self-coupling, or the interaction of the Higgs boson with the Higgs field, that gives the Higgs boson its mass. Now that the Higgs boson has been discovered, and we’re certain that the Higgs mechanism is the correct and valid explanation for how the Standard Model acquired its current structure, it’s no longer comprehensive and complete to say that there are “four fundamental forces” as we’ve so often said.

Instead, there’s a Higgs force as well. It isn’t so simple to measure this force as a push or pull between two particles, but it certainly exists and plays a role: weaker than the strong nuclear and electromagnetic forces, stronger than gravity, and perhaps somewhere more comparable to the magnitude of the weak nuclear force.

But that force is separate from the Higgs boson itself. The keys to remember when it comes to the Higgs boson is that:

  • it begins from an unbroken, four-component scalar,
  • when symmetry breaking occurs, those four components, or four degrees of freedom, lead to four scalar bosons,
  • three of them combine with the electroweak sector, giving the massive W-and-Z bosons, where the remaining electroweak combination yields the photon,
  • and then the last of those four degrees of freedom oscillates radially, creating the massive scalar particle known as the Higgs boson.

That’s as simple as I know how to make it without oversimplifying it in an incorrect way. I hope it helps you wrap your head around the Higgs boson just a little bit better! (And for more information and an additional perspective, I can recommend Matt Strassler’s excellent 2024 book, Waves in an Impossible Sea: How everyday life emerges from the cosmic ocean.)

item.title: Life is the most important problem in physics
item.description:
Descartes cut open living dogs and insisted their cries were just the noises of a machine. Astrophysicist and astrobiologist Adam Frank, a professor at the University of Rochester and author of The Little Book of Aliens, argues that the same life-as-machine metaphor still shapes how we think about AI, and that it gets life fundamentally wrong. Living things are self-creating, self-repairing systems that decide what matters to them, which is why he calls today’s AI an artificial mimic rather than an intelligence.

item.title: A medieval map mystery may finally be solved
item.description:
“We’ll just have to think our way back, step by step.” That’s what the Dutch geodesist Roelof Nicolai said in 2014 in a Strange Maps article. Nicolai had just spent his PhD years discovering that portolan charts — those gorgeous, wind-rose-covered coastline maps that suddenly appeared in Mediterranean ports in the second half of the 13th century — were geometrically too accurate to have been made the way everyone assumed. Something else was going on.

Twelve years on, we might have an answer. Tome Marelić, an assistant professor of geography at the University of Zadar in Croatia (and the current vice chair of the Working Group on the History of Cartography within the International Cartographic Association), has spent years doing exactly the step-by-step thinking Nicolai prescribed in 2014. Read together, his scientific articles amount to the most detailed forensic examination portolan charts have ever received. And the story they tell is more satisfying than even the more out-there theories (including “aliens did it”).

Mapping the Mediterranean

First, a quick refresher. A portolan chart is a nautical chart of the Mediterranean, western European, and northwest African coasts, criss-crossed with dense color-coded web-like networks often called “rhumb lines,” dotted with harbor names written perpendicular to the coast (so you had to keep spinning the chart to read it). The charts are calibrated with little beaded scale bars marking off distances in miglia, or so-called portolan miles whose roots remained enigmatic for decades until Marelić’s recently proposed explanation. (A Portolan mile is a bit shorter than a modern statute mile.)

The oldest surviving example, the anonymous Carte Pisane, appeared in Italy around 1270. Geometrically speaking, it looks like a finished product. There’s no awkward teenage phase of European cartography preceding it — no 13th-century equivalent of a flip phone before the smartphone. It just arrives, fully formed, with Mediterranean coastlines accurate enough to almost look like a map from today.

“The immense accuracy of coastline renderings on portolan charts, which, as far as is known, suddenly appeared in mid- to late-13th century, was never fully and objectively explained,” says Marelić.

Romantic and seemingly plausible — but wrong

The traditional explanation is romantic and, at first glance, plausible: Generations of sailors recorded their compass bearings and estimated distances in logbooks, and cartographers eventually compiled all that dead-reckoning data into a single chart. The trouble, as Nicolai discovered first, is that the numbers don’t work. Simulate a medieval ship captain’s best-effort compass-and-guesswork navigation, average enough of those readings together, and you get a chart ten times less accurate than the actual portolan chart.

This is where Marelić comes in. His method of choice is cartometric analysis — precise, computer-assisted measurements and error-computations. Take an old chart, digitize it, pin a few hundred identifiable points (ports, capes, river mouths, islands) to their true modern coordinates, and let the software calculate exactly how much the old map agrees with the modern map in a certain projection by scaling and rotating it until their geometrical best fit is obtained. The size of that remaining mismatch, expressed in measurable distance, tells you how accurate the chart really is, and even the exact magnitude and direction of errors for every pinned point. Random surveying errors should scatter every which way. Systemic errors, however, typically point to the map projection fabric in the background, which is sometimes, and especially in this case, invisible to the naked eye.

Marelić meticulously scrutinized that background fabric for years, stumbling upon some groundbreaking and intricate findings along the way.

Finding #1: Mosaics that defy the medieval origin narrative

Marelić confirmed and quantified that when you cut a portolan chart into regional bits — Western Mediterranean, Adriatic, Aegean, and so on — and georeference each bit separately, the accuracy roughly doubles compared to the map as a whole. That is what you’d expect if a cartographer had glued together several pre-existing charts of slightly different appearances into one seamless-looking whole.

Although portolan chart subsections, as he dubbed them, were detected by a few earlier scholars, Marelić originally computed that the earliest known pieces — such as the anonymous Pisane, Cortona, Lucca, and Avignon charts that are often treated as somewhat primitive — have portions of coastline that are nearly identical to those on allegedly more mature charts made by Genoese cartographer Pietro Vesconte in the early 14th century.

Even more intriguingly, his second article reveals that Vesconte’s charts remained the most accurate on a subsectional level for at least the next three centuries, while the third paper demonstrates that multi-sheet portolan atlases show the same pattern: images of seas that are geometrically frozen in time. Only this time, the atlases are mosaics within mosaics, with their subsections cut and sliced and arbitrarily encapsulated into sheets of varying map scales and coverages.

Tellingly, none of those authors seem to have fully understood the geometry of their own work, not even those who made portolan atlases, books that allow for more liberties to depict smaller regions than one-piece charts. Compare an atlas sheet to a portolan chart made by the very same cartographer, and even they don’t quite agree. These were not confident creators; they were copyists, doing their careful but imperfect best with material they didn’t fully understand.

Finding #2: The compass has an alibi

One of the more curious aspects of portolan charts is that their coastlines are all tilted roughly -10° off true north. The leading explanation has always been magnetic declination: Medieval sailors trusted their compasses, not realizing that magnetic north and true north aren’t quite the same thing — thus unknowingly infusing that error into every portolan chart.

It’s a neat story, but as Marelić found, it doesn’t hold water. He checked the theory against a paleomagnetic model of how Earth’s magnetic field actually behaved in the Mediterranean region between the late 13th and late 16th centuries. And the cartographic tilt doesn’t track with the magnetic reality of that era — not in degree, not in geography, not over time. Whatever initially rotated these coastlines, it wasn’t a 13th-century compass needle. In fact, his findings point to a completely different root cause: a late medieval graphical compromise between two map projections with significantly different appearances, both of which were developed about a millennium and a half before and long forgotten, but more on that later.

Finding #3: Medieval scholars point to Ancient Greece

Digging through historical sources, Marelić turned up three medieval witnesses who all, in their own words and independent of each other, say the same odd thing: that these charts came from an older time.

  • Persian polymath Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, writing in 1282 — a mere dozen years after the Carte Pisane surfaces — described a gridded crude map, geometrically almost identical to the Carte Pisane and the Cortona chart, that he attributes to the “sages of Greece and the ancient geometers.”
  • A chart from around 1360 carries an inscription crediting a shadowy figure called Rex Tholomeus — likely a garbled mashup of “king” and “Ptolemy” — who supposedly “measured the world” long ago for being the author of its source data.
  • A 1464 navigation manual by Ragusan merchant Benedetto Cotrugli says that Ptolemy made a world map from which “we have drawn a navigational chart” and that sailors of his day “owe him a lot because we do not wander [across the sea] today.”

Finding #4: The suspiciously specific mile

Every portolan chart uses the same basic unit of distance, the miglio, a mile generally reckoned at around 1.25 km. Nobody has ever satisfactorily explained where that particular number comes from. Marelić thinks he’s found it, and the culprit is, fittingly, a mistake.

Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose Geography dominated Western cartography during the Renaissance, underestimated Earth’s circumference by about 29%. Measure out two degrees of longitude along the Mediterranean’s mid-latitude using Ptolemy’s too-small Earth, and you get almost exactly 125 kilometers — which just so happens to be 100 portolan miles, the length of one grid square on these charts.

In other words: The miglio isn’t a freshly measured medieval nautical mile at all. It’s a fossil, the shadow of an ancient astronomer’s arithmetic error, smuggled across more than a thousand years and built into every portolan chart’s ruler.

Finding #5: At last, a name

Marelić’s most recent paper is his boldest: an attempt to reconstruct, step by step, exactly how a specific chart — the Carta Riccardiana, likely drawn by Pietro Vesconte sometime between 1300 and 1325 — might actually have been assembled.

Marelić suggests that Vesconte based his work on older regional maps drawn in the style of Marinus of Tyre (a 1st-century Greek-Roman geographer whose lost atlas was a major influence on Ptolemy). According to Marelić, Vesconte tried to combine these separate maps into a single map by enlarging some parts, changing their angles and positions, and joining them together. The result was an imperfect attempt to imitate Ptolemy’s more advanced map projection: a single curved map centred on Gibraltar.

In parallel, this discovery identifies the root cause of the well-known “Mercator effect” — the appearance of a geometrical pattern across every portolan chart of the Mediterranean and Black Sea areas that resembles the Mercator projection, long before it was established in 1569. That effect is the result of collating local maps made in equidistant cylindrical projection – a simpler technique than Mercator, which nonetheless can resemble that later projection when stitched together. This resolves the apparent paradox of the “Mercator projection before Mercator,” which previously puzzled some scholars — even Marelić himself, in earlier stages of his research.

Lay all of Marelić’s studies end to end, and a single picture emerges. The portolan chart wasn’t a eureka moment of 13th-century Italian seamanship. It was a very good copy — or, more precisely, different copies — of cartographic knowledge that was already ancient before the Middle Ages even began, filtered through at least one confused but conscientious medieval hand, and finally dressed up with compass roses and scale bars to look shipshape for a new seafaring age.

Medieval sailors didn’t make these accurate maps. As they navigated the waters of their Mediterranean world, they were unwittingly standing on the shoulders of giants.

Back in 2014, Nicolai laughingly waved off the idea that lost civilizations had left behind the first portolan chart, the way you might snub a conspiracy theorist at a dinner party. Marelić’s five papers are, in a sense, the long-delayed main course for that dinner.

His findings require no spaceships, no lost super-civilization. Just Ancient knowledge, imperfectly transmitted by medieval copyists, intriguing enough to baffle modern humans.

Sometimes the most satisfying ending to a cold case isn’t a twist-and-reveal; it’s the meticulous piecing together of all the evidence hidden in the source material – one portolan mile at a time.

+ + +

We had the chance to ask Professor Marelić himself about the motivation for his research and the meaning of his discoveries. The following Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.

What first drew you to portolan charts?

“In short, it’s the mystery of their origin, which is one of the biggest unresolved questions in the history of cartography. They are out-of-place artefacts, the cartographic equivalent of the Antikythera mechanism.”

“I first learned about portolan charts via Charles Hapgood’s Maps of the Ancient Sea Kings when I was still in elementary school, back in the late 1990s. The subject was too complex for me to understand as a kid, but I was very impressed by the images of those old charts that were drawn so accurately.”

“The mystery lay dormant until my PhD studies decades later, when I cartometrically examined the accuracy of Adriatic Sea renderings on portolan charts. I realized that Hapgood’s theory of ancient lost civilisations as creators of the source maps is implausible. Many historians of cartography regard his book as pseudoscience. I don’t fully share that negative view: I believe his curiosity was pure, and I admire his pioneering audacity to use quantitative analysis on charts, even though they weren’t conducted with due diligence.”

“Then I started applying my analytical approach to the entire area covered by portolan charts, from the Atlantic to the Black Sea. And here we are, roughly four years and five peer-reviewed journal articles later.”

“The two most influential sources for my work are the doctoral dissertations of Scott Allen Loomer, from 1987, and Roel Nicolai, from 2014. Theirs are among the most extensive and intricate cartometric studies of portolan charts. What kept me going was the incompleteness of their results, and the occasional overcomplexity of their methods.”

“That incompleteness is very normal in scientific research, as well as understandable, since they didn’t have any historical evidence of pre-medieval origins. In contrast, I discovered Benedetto Cotrugli’s 1464 mention of an origin in classical Antiquity early on in my PhD research, and it fed my belief that there were other similar sources around. Luckily, that proved a good hunch.”

“Besides, I gradually came to think that the overcomplexity of some of the existing methods leads nowhere. I thought that if those charts were made by late medieval illustrators who didn’t understand map projections, some blatantly simple explanation for their geometry must be lurking somewhere in the dark. This suspicion eventually led me to what is probably the decoding of the portolan mile length and the mechanics of portolan chart assembly.”

Your work sits between geodesy, the history of science and the history of navigation. What did you have to teach yourself along the way?

“My pre-PhD degrees are in geography, a discipline that examines the environment and the world itself in a holistic manner. Also prior to my PhD, I developed decent GIS software skills and an understanding of various projected coordinate systems in the GIS environment and their applications. Combined with my curiosity about the history of technology and science, formed the foundation for this interdisciplinary research on portolan charts, which can be classified as digital humanities.”

Cotrugli, one of your key witnesses, was a Ragusan (i.e. from Dubrovnik), so basically a neighbor of yours. Did that geographic kinship add a personal touch to your work?

“Also known as Benedikt Kotruljević in Croatian, Cotrugli is most renowned for his book Of commerce and the perfect merchant, which contains the first description of double-entry bookkeeping in history. While it’s cool on a personal level to share a homeland with such a consequential figure, on a professional level, I interpret his writings as objectively as those of Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, the Persian scholar whose records fall in the same camp as Cotrugli’s.”

Exactly what could a late-medieval navigator do with a portolan chart that they couldn’t do without one? In other words, What made these maps so valuable?

“The charts are a topologically fairly accurate representation, thus they give a good “big-picture” insight into Mediterranean sub-basins and other areas. So at the very least, they could have served as graphical confirmation of the topology that sailors had memorised.”

“However, this doesn’t work the other way around: the mental topologies memorised by navigators could not have produced charts of such accuracy on their own – the areas are too large, and the Earth’s curvature must be factored in. In other words: you’d need to start with a proper survey. And that survey could not be conducted with dead reckoning, because that method would lead to an accumulation of errors greater than those detected in portolan chart geometry.”

“Contrary to their – limited – usefulness, portolan charts have a number of features that could have made them death traps for navigators who trusted them blindly.”

“First, most of the charted area was not aligned with the magnetic declination prevailing when they were made. This limited their usefulness for sailing by compass, and that problem increased over time as the (easterly) declination decreased while the chart image remained unchanged.”

“Scales varied regionally, numerous transitions in coastline geometry reduced accuracy, and their generally small scale – often around 1:5,000,000 – made them poorly suited to navigating coasts dense with islands. Also, coastlines were crudely simplified, and especially the earliest charts contain no inland geographical information. The absence of isolated prominent landmarks like Mount Etna, which would have been visible from ships before the ports at its base, reduced navigational usefulness, and is a further argument against a medieval origin.”

In plain terms, what is the single most important thing your research has revealed about these charts that nobody knew before?

“If I had to choose one discovery, it would be the mechanics of portolan chart assembly proposed in my latest paper. But that would overlook the work of my earlier papers, because each added important pieces to the puzzle.”

“The first paper showed that the earliest anonymous charts, which are considered less advanced, contain coastline sections almost identical to those on Pietro Vesconte’s charts, which are considered more mature. This suggests that they all copied the same source material.”

“The second paper showed that Vesconte’s charts are the most accurate at the regional level over a period of three centuries. It also brought together, for the first time, three historical accounts claiming that portolan charts originated in classical antiquity.”

“The third paper provided the first cartometric analysis of portolan atlases. It showed that they are essentially portolan chart images arbitrarily split into physically separate pieces, and exposed extensive evidence against a medieval origin.”

“The fourth paper marked a shift towards positive evidence for an origin in Classical Antiquity. It quantitatively analysed Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi’s description of a map made by Greek sages and ancient geometers, identifying numerical evidence supporting his claim. It also proposed that the mysterious portolan mile was a late-medieval byproduct of treating Ptolemy’s inaccurate longitude intervals as distances and applying them to a relatively accurate geometric representation of the Mediterranean.”

“Finally, the fifth paper identified, for the first time, the geometrical fingerprints of Marinus of Tyre and an additional set of Ptolemy’s fingerprints in portolan chart geometry. It also proposed the simplest model yet for how portolan charts were assembled, one consistent with the historical development of map projections, and explaining the root cause of the so-called “Mercator effect” across the Mediterranean.”

Across several papers and years of work, what for you was the most surprising result?

“Two results spring to mind. The first one is the realisation that 50 portolan miles – a typical large interval on portolan chart scale bars – correspond to one degree of longitude along the Mediterranean’s mid-parallel, according to Ptolemy’s inaccurately perceived size of the Earth. The second is that typical portolan chart geometry, including the so-called “Mercator effect”, can be achieved by partially enlarging some source maps and rotating them by half a magnitude relative to the spatial layout on Ptolemy’s projection, moving eastward from Gibraltar.”

“Because these findings are based on simple and straightforward maths, reasoning or logic – whatever you want to call it – I couldn’t help but be surprised and amazed by the fact that no one had ever thought of it before. And, for that matter, that it hadn’t occurred to myself earlier.”

We may never be able to pin down the exact source with certainty, but if you had to put your money on it: where, when and with whom do you think the now-lost maps behind the portolan charts did first originate?

“Indeed! Even though the portolan chart origin story is increasingly coherent and less anachronistic as my research progresses – probably to the disappointment of those searching for more exotic origins in long-lost civilisations – my findings do still not provide definitive answers. What they do make clear, however, is that Greco-Roman science and technology were of a much higher level than we currently know, and that in itself is a fascinating conclusion, inviting more research.”

“If I was to bet on the most likely place and time of origin, I would say the Roman Empire at its greatest territorial extent, under Trajan, around 100 AD. Why? Two reasons. One is that the boundaries of the Empire at that time coincide almost perfectly with the typical coverage of portolan charts. The other is that this was the only time in history when the entire area covered by those charts was under a unified political authority with both an interest in mapping its territory, and the means and knowledge to do so to the same high standard of accuracy. Those conditions are missing from any period before or after.”

Strange Maps #1204

item.title: The first DNA crime test didn’t catch the killer. It freed an innocent man.
item.description:
The events leading to the first forensic DNA case began in 1983. Lynda Mann was only 15 years old when, returning home from babysitting one evening in the Leicestershire village of Narborough, she was raped and murdered as she took a shortcut along a footpath known by villagers as the Black Pad. It was a path that would be unlikely to be known by anyone who wasn’t local, suggesting the killer was someone from the area.

At the time, the biological side of forensic science was still in its infancy, though there were a handful of tests that could help narrow things down in terms of identifying the perpetrator. Investigators could determine from a semen sample that he was blood group A, which is the case for about 40% of the English population. Having established his blood group, they were able to tell that he was a “secretor,” which is true for about 70% of the population. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) enzyme testing was also carried out. PGM is an enzyme that both men and women carry, and it comes in a number of different forms; hence, determining which type the perpetrator had could also help narrow things down. The perpetrator was found to be type PGM1+, alongside around 40% of people with European ancestry living in England.  

As this combination of factors would be found in around 10% of all men, it was clearly not enough to identify the killer, though it would prove to be useful information a few years later. But for the time being, despite a huge police investigation, including door-to-door inquiries in Narborough and the nearby villages of Enderby and Littlethorpe, the trail eventually went cold. 

Then, in 1986, another young girl, Dawn Ashworth, was also raped and murdered just off another footpath, Ten Pound Lane, this time in Enderby, very close to Narborough. As in Lynda’s case, the killer’s modus operandi pointed to someone with local knowledge of the area: both the crimes took place in a part of each village that only locals were likely to know about. The similarities in both cases led the police to link the two crimes. There was a serial killer on the loose. 

Then came the first twist in the story, and with it, the first time that DNA “fingerprinting” would be used in a forensic case. Richard Buckland, a kitchen porter, aged 17 at the time and with learning difficulties, had been seen in the area on a motorbike, similar to the one that had been seen in the area when Dawn went missing. He also seemed to know, even before the police did, where Dawn might be found. The police brought him in and, under questioning, Richard confessed to Dawn’s murder, but he staunchly protested his innocence when it came to the second murder: He had not killed Lynda. 

With Richard in custody, the police were in a quandary. They were pretty convinced they had their suspect for both cases, but they needed new evidence to break the deadlock and also connect Richard to Lynda’s murder. The detective chief superintendent of the Leicestershire Police at the time, David Baker, had read an article in the local newspaper, the Leicester Mercury, about the work of [geneticist and DNA “fingerprinting” pioneer] Alec Jeffreys in the Sarbah case [of matching a mother and son’s DNA]. David had a brainwave.  

The police are always looking for new ways to help solve cases, and he recognized that this new technique could be used forensically: DNA fingerprinting could take this broad biological categorization of the perpetrator from being from a group of about 10% of the population, right down to “a group of one.” And if it could do that, it would confirm whether Richard Buckland had killed both girls, and he would go to jail for his crimes. 

In the meantime, Alec and his team were fine-tuning the DNA fingerprinting process. While the patterns of blobs and lines generated in the first version of DNA fingerprinting were ideal for telling individuals apart from one another, they were extremely complicated and difficult to explain in court. Alec’s team had been homing in on just some of these genetic stutters to understand more about them. They had been finding more and more of them across the genome, each following the same pattern — a DNA “word” repeated over and over again many times. It wasn’t the same word as before, however, but lots of different words, each of them tandemly repeated over and over again, and some were highly variable. There tends to be a standard range of repeats that you find in a population — say, between 10 and 27. So far from seeing only three possible combinations, the number of possible combinations was in the many hundreds for one marker alone. The team homed in on markers with considerable variation in the number of repeats an individual might have, making them perfect candidates for developing a more convenient test for casework. 

Concentrating on these markers, fine-tuning and polishing the technique, was starting to give what the forensic community, and courts, would want: something that was quick to carry out, easy to interpret (important when explaining things to a jury) but still highly specific in terms of telling individuals apart. It became known as DNA profiling. Alongside this, Alec had published a paper showing that DNA could be extracted not only from bloodstains up to four years old, but also from semen stains. 

In another breakthrough, it was now possible to separate sperm cells from vaginal cells and extract DNA from them; hence, DNA fingerprinting could be used to identify the perpetrator in a rape case. Each incremental scientific discovery was slowly leading towards the much-needed breakthrough in the hunt for Dawn and Lynda’s killer. 

Just as there was progress on the scientific front, so there was in the police investigation. Like Alec, David Baker could see the potential of linking DNA with forensics, and he was about to give Alec his first case. Between them, they would make history not once, but twice. 

DNA fingerprinting could take this broad biological categorization of the perpetrator from being from a group of about 10% of the population, right down to ‘a group of one.’

David’s request was simple. Convinced that there would be a DNA match, he asked Alec if he would run a DNA fingerprinting test on Richard Buckland and then on the samples taken from Lynda. A DNA match linking Richard to Lynda would provide the evidence linking him to her murder as well — both cases would be solved in one fell swoop. 

Alec agreed to run the test, and samples from Lynda and Richard Buckland were transferred to his lab just weeks later. This was to be his first ever forensic case and Alec was fully aware of the importance of what he was doing. Within a few days, he knew the DNA testing had worked, and he had his results. It was time to ring David with the news — both good and bad. 

The good news was that the DNA analysis had worked, but the bad news was that Richard Buckland’s DNA had not been found with Lynda’s. Lynda’s killer and Richard had completely different DNA fingerprints: The police had identified the wrong suspect for that murder. David then asked Alec to repeat the process with samples from Dawn. Again, the news was both good and bad: The DNA testing was successful, but it showed that, despite Richard’s confession, he hadn’t killed Dawn either. The young lad in custody was completely innocent of the crimes he was thought to have committed. On November 21, 1986, three years to the day since Lynda had been murdered, Richard Buckland was duly released. Thus the first time that DNA fingerprinting was used in a criminal case, rather than establishing the suspect’s guilt, as anticipated, it proved their innocence and exonerated them of a crime. Without it, Richard would have been wrongly imprisoned for a double murder, almost certainly spending decades in prison for crimes he hadn’t committed.* 

And while Richard Buckland was the first, he certainly hasn’t been the last in all the years since then. The Innocence Project states that, in the United States, at the time of writing, 203 people have been proved to be wrongly convicted on the basis of DNA evidence, including several individuals on death row. Statistics like these help underline the profound implications of the technology pioneered by Alec and his team. 

* Author’s Note: DNA forensic evidence would later be used again to help identify Lynda and Dawn’s killer, Colin Pitchfork.

item.title: 3 original methods for measuring the distance to the stars
item.description:
Out there in space, blazing just a scant 150 million kilometers away lies the brightest and most massive object in our Solar System: the Sun. Shining hundreds of thousands of times as bright in Earth’s skies as the next brightest object, the full Moon, the Sun is unique among Solar System objects for producing its own visible light, rather than only appearing illuminated because of reflected light. However, the thousands upon thousands of stars visible in the night sky — escalating into the millions and billions when we aid our vision with telescopes and cameras — are all also self-luminous, distinguishing themselves from the planets and other Solar System objects in that regard.

But how far away are they?

Unlike the planets, Sun, and Moon, the stars appear to remain fixed in their position over time: not only from night-to-night but also throughout the year and even from year-to-year. We even call it “the fixed background of stars” when measuring the motion of objects within our Solar System against them. Compared to the objects in our own Solar System, the stars must be incredibly far away. And therefore, in order to be seen from such great distances, they must be incredibly intrinsically bright.

It only makes sense to assume, as many did dating back to antiquity, that those stars must be Sun-like objects located at great distances from us. But how far away are they? It wasn’t until the 1600s that we got our first answers, one each from three titans of physics history:

  • Robert Hooke,
  • Christiaan Huygens,
  • and Isaac Newton.

Unsurprisingly, those early answers didn’t agree with one another, but who came closest to getting it correct, and whose methods helped us the most in the centuries to come? The story is as educational as it is fascinating.

The first method: Robert Hooke

The simplest, most straightforward and direct way to measure the distances to the stars is one that dates back thousands of years: the notion of stellar parallax. The idea is the same one as the phenomenon behind the game we all play as children, where you:

  • close one eye,
  • hold your thumb up at arm’s length from you,
  • then switch which eye is closed and which one is open,
  • and watch your thumb shift relative to the objects farther away in the background.

Whenever you have two different vantage points to look from (such as each of your two eyes), objects that are close by will appear to “shift” relative to the objects that are farther away. This phenomenon, known as parallax, could theoretically be used to measure the distances to any of the stars, but would be most easily leveraged for the closest stars of all.

At least, that would be true under the assumption that the stars are actually close enough to appear to shift, given the limitations of our bodies, our equipment, and our vantage point. In ancient times, people assumed that the cosmos was geocentric, so they attempted to observe parallax by looking at the same stars at dawn and at dusk, seeing if a baseline distance of one Earth diameter (as the Earth rotates over that 12 hour span) between the two observing points would lead to an observable shift in any stars. As it turns out, no such shift is detectable.

However, in the 1600s, after the work of Copernicus, Galileo, and Kepler revealed a heliocentric model to our Universe, scientist Robert Hooke thought the parallax method might now at last bear fruit.

In the late 1660s, Hooke went for it. He knew that atmospheric refraction (or the bending of light rays due to Earth’s atmosphere) might be a problem, so to minimize that effect, he built what’s known as a zenith telescope: a telescope that looked straight up overhead, minimizing the amount of Earth’s atmosphere that light would need to travel through. Measuring the position of Gamma Draconis — the zenith star as visible from his location in London, England — Hooke took multiple observations of the star over the course of the year, looking for any apparent shift in its position from “true zenith,” to the best precision his instruments could muster.

He recorded four measurements beginning in 1669, and noticed a variation that he claimed was observable with the precision of his instruments: 25 arc-seconds, or about 0.007 degrees. He published his results in An Attempt to Prove the Motions of Earth by Observations in 1674, wherein he wrote:

“Tis manifest then by the observations … that there is a sensible parallax of Earth’s Orb to the fixt Star in the head of Draco, and consequently a confirmation of the Copernican System against the Ptolomaick [Ptolemaic] and Tichonick [Tychonic].”

The inferred distance to Gamma Draconis, according to Hooke’s measurements, would work out to about 0.26 light-years, or 16,500 times the Earth-Sun distance. When compared against the modern result, it turns out that Hooke’s measurements were way off; Gamma Draconis is actually 154 light-years away and has a parallax of only 21 milli-arc-seconds, or over a factor of 1000 smaller than Hooke’s measurement.

The second method: Christiaan Huygens

Many astronomers, throughout the 17th century and even earlier, had a very different idea for how to estimate the distances to the stars.

  • First, you assume that the Sun is a typical star, with a typical intrinsic brightness and size.
  • Then, you measure the relative brightness of the Sun compared to the observed brightness of a star in the night sky.
  • And finally, you use the fact that brightness falls off as one-over-the-distance-squared (an inverse square law, as shown above) to calculate how much farther away those stars are than the Sun is.

The problem that everyone who attempted to leverage such a method faced, however, was the difficulty of that second step. Given that the Sun is so incredibly bright and the stars — even the brightest among them — are so incredibly faint, a fair comparison seemed practically impossible. Beyond that, you can only see the stars at night, when the Sun has set, so a side-by-side, simultaneous comparison is practically impossible.

That’s where Huygens came in. He began with a long, opaque, large-aperture tube, and viewed the brightest star in the night sky through it: Sirius. He then fastened a light-blocking brass disk over the edge of the tube, but drilled a number of holes in it: for use during the daytime. Huygens realized that if he could drill holes that were smaller and smaller, only allowing a tiny, minuscule fraction of the Sun’s light through — even smaller than a pinprick — he could eventually create a hole so small that it would have the same brightness to his eyes as Sirius did the night before.

Unfortunately for Huygens, even the smallest hole he was able to drill in his brass disk left him with a tiny dot of sunlight that was far, far brighter than any of the stars he saw. What he did, then, was to insert, into the smallest of the holes he drilled, tiny glass beads that would further fainten the sunlight that filtered through it, dimming its brightness by still greater amounts.

Compared to the full, unfiltered light from the Sun, Huygens calculated that he had to reduce its brightness — with a combination of blocking most of the Sun’s disk and putting a mostly opaque (but slightly transparent) bead in the tiny hole within the brass disk — by a factor of 765.3 million (765,300,000) in order to match the same brightness that Sirius would possess at night. Because brightness falls off as one over the distance squared, that means the square root of that number would tell him how much farther away the star in question (Sirius) would be as compared to the Earth-Sun distance: a factor of 27,664.

That works out to 0.44 light-years, or 27,664 times the Earth-Sun distance. This is farther than Hooke’s estimate for Gamma Draconis, but relies on a key assumption: that Sirius is the same brightness as the Sun. It turns out that Sirius isn’t quite Sun-like, but intrinsically is an A-star as opposed to a G-star like our Sun. In detail, it’s approximately 25.4 times brighter than the Sun. If Huygens had known that fact, he would have computed the distance to be 2.2 light-years: somewhat closer to the actual distance of 8.6 light-years, which wasn’t bad for an estimate made back in 1698!

The third method: Isaac Newton

Way back in 1668, a contemporary and friend of Isaac Newton, James Gregory, wrote a treatise entitled Geometriae pars universalis, where he came up with an ingenious method that, quite arguably, was superior to Huygens’ method for measuring the relative brightness of the Sun to the stars: to use a planet as an intermediary. If you can find a planet in our Solar System whose brightness matches the brightness of a star precisely, and you observe that planet at that particular instant, then there’s a straightforward method for comparing the distances within the Solar System to the distance to the matching star. All you have to do is the following:

  • calculate how far the light had to travel and “spread out” from the Sun before hitting the planet,
  • know how much of the sunlight that strikes the planet gets reflected (its albedo, or reflectivity),
  • know the diameter (i.e., physical size) of the planet that’s being observed,
  • and then calculate how the reflected light from the planet spreads out before it reaches your eyes.

Gregory did a preliminary calculation himself, but warned that it would be untrustworthy until better estimates of Solar System distances were known.

Although Gregory (perhaps more famous, historically, for designing the Gregorian telescope) would die young (at the age of 36) in 1674, Newton possessed a copy of his book and became quite familiar with it, and worked out a more precise version of Gregory’s calculations, perhaps as early as 1685 by some estimations. It was only after Newton’s death in 1727, however, that his final manuscript was collected and published, seeing the light of day in 1728 under the title of The System of the World (De mundi systemate), even though it was originally intended to be the third volume of his much more famous Principia Mathematica.

The advantages to using Gregory’s methods were clear:

  • you could observe a star (such as Sirius) and whatever planet you chose for comparison simultaneously, rather than having to rely on your memory from hours earlier to compare brightnesses,
  • you could observe them under similar observing conditions, especially when the star and planet were close together in the sky,
  • and, in the aftermath of Newton’s laws and with Newton’s reflecting telescope, it would be possible to both know the distance to the planets and also their physical size at that distance through direct measurements.

Although Gregory performed his initial estimates using Jupiter as a calibration point, Newton instantly recognized that Saturn, being the most distant known planet from the Sun at the time, would provide a better baseline. (There are limitations, though: Jupiter always appears brighter than Sirius and Saturn always appears fainter than Sirius, so perhaps Sirius, despite being the brightest star, wasn’t the best star to choose for comparison.) Based on observations by John Flamsteed in 1672, Newton knew that Saturn was about 9-to-10 times farther away from the Sun than Earth, and was also about 10 times larger, in diameter, than Earth is.

What Newton didn’t know, however, was how reflective Saturn was (i.e., what its albedo was; he guessed it reflected 50% of the light that struck it), and he also didn’t know — just like Huygens — how intrinsically bright Sirius was (he, too, assumed it was identical to the Sun). His answer was larger than that of either Huygens or Hooke: about 300,000 times the Earth-Sun distance, or in modern terms, about 4.7 light-years.

Evaluating the three methods

From these early estimates dating back 300 years or more, we had three famed scientists, three independent methods, and three quite different answers for the distances to the stars. So how far away are the stars, really?

Huygens’s and Newton’s methods, while very clever given the limited instrumental capabilities available to them during their lives, suffered from a big problem: you needed to know something intrinsic about the brightness of the stars you were observing relative to the Sun, which is information that astronomers would not possess until the 20th century. Whereas Huygens underestimated the distance to Sirius even after you account for its larger intrinsic brightness than the Sun, if you apply that same correction to Newton’s method, it turns out that he significantly overestimated the distance to Sirius; Gregory’s original, admittedly unreliable estimate (of 83,190 times the Earth-Sun distance, or 1.32 light-years) actually turned out to be better than Newton’s, because if you correct for the actual intrinsic brightness of Sirius, it yields a distance estimate of 6.6 light-years: a difference of just 23% from the true value!

Hooke, on the other hand, may have been off by the greatest amount, but his method is the one that has led to the most successful and widespread of applications as far as measuring stellar distances goes in our modern era.

How did Hooke mess up so badly? It turns out that he must have grossly misinterpreted what he was observing. As science historian Thony Christie documents, scientist James Bradley went through a painstaking attempt to reproduce Hooke’s experiment using multiple high-precision telescopes constructed explicitly for this purpose in 1725, using both his own house and the house of Samuel Molyneaux, his neighbor, for independent verification. Again, they went to observe that same star that Hooke observed: Gamma Draconis.

Fascinatingly, Bradley actually did observe that the star’s position was seen to change, albeit slightly, over the course of a year. In fact, the star traced out a tiny ellipse, which is the shape you might expect, since the Earth orbits around the Sun in an elliptical path: something that had been known since the time of Kepler in the early 1600s. But Bradley, careful as he was, noted that this couldn’t be due to stellar parallax for an important reason: the changes in position were in the wrong direction! As Christie wrote back in 2010,

“Bradley knew that this was not parallax because the changes in position were in the wrong directions, when according to the parallax theory the star should have moved south it moved north and vice versa. Bradley could not believe his own results and spent another year meticulously repeating his observations; the result was the same.”

What could be causing this motion? Unbeknownst to Bradley at the time, he had just discovered the phenomenon of stellar aberration: where celestial objects appear to shift position based on the motion of the observer. In the case of Gamma Draconis as seen from Earth, the motion of the observer is largely driven by the motion of the Earth around the Sun at a speed of around ~30 km/s, or about 0.01% the speed of light. Although it was sufficient to prove that Earth does, indeed, orbit around the Sun, it was no detection of parallax at all.

Parallax wouldn’t be detected until the 1830s, when three separate astronomers — Thomas Henderson, Friedrich Bessel, and Wilhelm Struve — looking at three different stars (Alpha Centauri, 61 Cygni, and Vega, respectively) all detected an actual motion throughout the year, definitively measuring stellar parallax. Although Henderson made his observations first, in 1833, he didn’t publish his results until 1839. Meanwhile, Struve had preliminary but unreliable (and ultimately, incorrect) data about Vega that he published in 1837, and wouldn’t publish a superior, more correct measurement until 1840. Meanwhile, Bessel published his high-quality data on November 5, 1838, and is generally regarded as the discoverer of the first stellar parallax.

The true game-changing invention would be the development of photography as applied to astronomy, which led to the first photographs of the Moon and Sun in the 1840s and, eventually, the first photograph of a star in 1850. Being able to compare photographs, initially by eye and now in a computerized fashion, has led to the modern measurement of more than a billion stellar parallaxes here in the Milky Way, with the European Space Agency’s Gaia satellite responsible for the overwhelming majority of those measurements. Parallax, not brightness measurements, are the way to actually measure the distance to the stars.

Of the three early estimates made, however, Hooke’s claimed “parallax” distance was by far the worst. While Huygens and Newton were within an order of magnitude of the correct answer (once one corrects for intrinsic stellar brightness), Hooke’s measurements were off by more than a factor of 1000! In fact, Hooke’s chosen star — Gamma Draconis — despite being relatively bright, did not have a non-zero parallax detected until the Hipparcos Catalogue was published in 1997, revealing its modern distance of 154 light-years. Although, as humans, we tend to value getting the right answer regardless of the method used, in science, it’s the procedure that one follows, and the reproducibility of the correct answer, that truly matters as far as establishing validity goes.

This article was first published in February of 2024. It was updated in November of 2026.

item.title: The more you know, the harder it is to change someone’s mind
item.description:
Here’s the bad news: The deeper your understanding of an issue and the stronger your conviction about the solution, the worse you often become at persuasion. This isn’t a character flaw; it’s a law of neuroscience. Once you understand it, you’ll stop wondering why your brilliant ideas and proposals keep floundering in meeting rooms. It’s due to a cognitive trap that the fields of behavioral economics and neuroscience have spent decades documenting: the curse of knowledge. Once I explain how it works, you’ll start to recognize why it’s working against your persuasion.

In the early 1990s, Stanford graduate student Elizabeth Newton designed a simple experiment that revealed something profound about human cognition. She divided participants into two groups: “tappers” and “listeners.” Tappers were given a list of well-known songs like “Happy Birthday to You” and “The Star-Spangled Banner” — simple tunes everyone knows. They were asked to tap out a song’s rhythm on a table while a listener tried to identify it. Before they began, tappers were asked to predict how often listeners would correctly identify the song. The tappers predicted a 50% success rate — after all, these were famous songs, and the rhythms were distinctive. They felt confident they could tap them out clearly. The actual success rate? Out of 120 songs tapped, listeners correctly identified only 3 — a success rate of 2.5%.

This result shocked the tappers. The rhythm was clear and unmistakable to them as they tapped. How could the listeners not hear the song perfectly? What the tappers didn’t realize was that they had a fundamentally different experience from their listeners. When you tap out “Happy Birthday to You,” you hear the melody in your head. The song is complete and vivid in your mind. The listeners, however, hear something completely different: disconnected taps, with no underlying melody. They’re trying to identify a song from percussion alone, which is nearly impossible even for familiar tunes.

Here’s the frustrating part: The tapper cannot experience what the listener is experiencing in the moment. Once you hear the melody, you cannot tap the rhythm without that melody playing in your head, but the listener hears only the taps. In other words, your knowledge has fundamentally altered your perception of what you believe others are experiencing. This is the curse of knowledge. And it doesn’t just apply to tapping songs. It applies to your persuasion, especially when you are the well-informed expert in the room. As you are about to learn from three economists, experts are lousy at thinking like their audiences.

Why experts fail to persuade

Economists Colin Camerer, George Loewenstein, and Martin Weber published a paper that challenged beliefs about how informed people predict the judgment of less-informed people. Economic models assumed that experts could accurately anticipate how novices would think. The researchers discovered something very surprising, however: Experts were systematically biased predictors. Building on psychologist Baruch Fischhoff’s earlier work on hindsight bias — the tendency to believe, once you know an outcome, that you would have predicted it all along — they found that once someone acquired knowledge or expertise, they became anchored in that more-informed state of mind. When asked to predict what someone without that knowledge would think or do, experts could not mentally set aside what they knew. They were pulled inevitably toward their informed perspective rather than the other person’s.

This curse of knowledge functions like a cognitive undertow. It becomes extraordinarily difficult to escape back to the state of not knowing, even temporarily and even when it would serve you to do so — especially when it comes to persuasion.

Here’s how this curse blindsides you in persuasion. You’ve spent weeks developing a proposal to solve a complex problem. You’ve acquired deep knowledge about the problem as well as considered several solutions and their trade-offs. You’ve thought through objections and counterarguments. You’ve found evidence that makes one solution stand out above the others. You’re now completely convinced of the way forward. By the time you present your proposal to decision-makers, you’re already deep in the curse of knowledge. You cannot accurately imagine what your proposal sounds like to anyone who’s encountering it for the first time. You cannot appreciate their state of ignorance or alternate perspective because you’re anchored in your state of knowledge.

While you need to simplify, translate, and educate your decision-makers, you instead persuade from the perspective of complexity and conviction. The various cognitive traps associated with the curse of knowledge distance you from your stakeholders’ perspectives, pushing you away from genuine engagement and ultimately leading you to persuasive impotence.

Now you can start to understand the baffling experience all of us have had: presenting what feels like an obvious and clear case for an idea and watching it hit a brick wall. From our perspective, everything is clear, logical, and persuasive. From our stakeholders’ perspective, we’re tapping out a rhythm to a song they can’t hear. What is playing in our heads — all that analysis, all those supporting arguments and evidence — is inaudible to them.

To further complicate matters, we become invested in a solution — “our” solution. Pride of ownership deepens our commitment. When stakeholders start to raise challenging questions, we say to ourselves: They must not be listening carefully. They must be resistant to change or protective of the status quo. The possibility that we’ve failed to build a bridge from their knowledge to ours doesn’t even occur to us, because we cannot see the gap.

The antidote to the curse of knowledge

There is an antidote to overcoming these psychological traps, but it requires a dramatic reframing of your understanding of the act of persuasion. You must abandon your mental model of persuasion as first and foremost a solution-centric activity*. Yes, at some point, you will start championing a particular solution, but only after an intensive exploration into the problem as well as its impact on key stakeholders. The core lesson here is that masterful persuasion starts with problem definition — not solution definition.

It’s not an easy perspective to accept. After all, you want to solve a problem efficiently and quickly. And who can resist the ego rewards of “pride of ownership” and the public recognition of how clever you are? Instead, with problem-centric persuasion, you’ll experience a different kind of reward: meaningful collaborations with colleagues in solving truly thorny problems. But this approach requires far more from your curiosity and skills of engagement, and — at the start — far less from your expertise and skills of advocacy.

Not so surprisingly, one of the trademark traits of leaders who are masterful at persuasion is that they’re instinctually curious. Before they try to change your mind, they work to understand it.

Truly effective persuasion begins with curiosity, not certainty. It begins with questions, not answers. It begins with exploring problems, not advocating solutions. As noted, later in the process, you will make a pitch and advocate for a particular solution. But this will occur only after you’ve gathered intelligence and built a rich understanding of the problem through others. Then you absolutely need to advance a clear recommendation. But the sequence matters profoundly. Questions first, pitches second.

Not so surprisingly, one of the trademark traits of leaders who are masterful at persuasion is that they’re instinctually curious. Before they try to change your mind, they work to understand it. They ask about your concerns, your priorities, your constraints, your resources, your values. Foundational to their curiosity is their capacity to listen. One of the most skillful persuasive leaders I’ve ever known said to me: “When I am most effective at persuasion, I’m spending 90% of my time listening and 10% talking.”

After he made this bold assertion, I decided to watch him in action. This is what I observed. When he had an idea or initiative he wanted to champion, he’d start with one-on-one meetings with colleagues, asking them questions and listening carefully. Together they would deep-dive into the problem he wanted to tackle. A set of simple exploratory questions would always kick off the process: Do you see this as a problem? What’s behind it? Do you feel it’s a pressing problem, or is it something we can put off? Why haven’t we successfully addressed it to date? How would you approach solving it? Who needs to get behind any solution? Who’s likely to oppose it? Who would be implementing any solution? What are the resources that might be needed, and are they at hand?

This approach built around questioning and listening remains counterintuitive for most people. The pitch reflex is too deeply embedded. It takes a conscious effort to resist. Listen first, advocate second.

* Author’s Note: The one exception here would be clients who are explicitly seeking your expertise to solve a problem only you know how to solve.
