item.title: A fake Einstein quote actually explains the affordability crisis
item.description:
One of the most famous quotes commonly attributed to Einstein was something that he himself never actually said: “Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn’t, pays it.” While the quote is not from Einstein at all, the math behind the concept of compound interest is incredibly profound, playing a role in any system — physical, mathematical, or financial — that accumulates based on how much of a base amount is present. When the base amount increases, it isn’t just the original amount (the principal) that continues to accumulate, but the additional amount (the interest) that adds to the accumulation as well.

While investors most often use this to explain the growth of wealth in an interest-bearing account, it can be applied not just to wealth, but to the cost and price of goods and commodities that continue to increase over time as well. When wealth increases, we call it compound interest, but when prices increase, we call it inflation: not the cosmic kind, but the economic kind. The Einstein quote may be a fake, or at least grossly misattributed, but if you want to understand the current affordability crisis, the mathematics and the concept behind the quote is exactly what everyone should understand. Here’s how it works.

The story behind the quote

Einstein grew to fame in the early 20th century, and died in 1955. While an enormous amount of his writings, speeches, and interviews survive, nothing that he ever said or wrote relating to compound interest survives. The earliest assertion that the quote was said by Einstein can be traced back to a 1983 New York Times column, which mentions the quote as a popular saying that’s attributed to him. But it’s likely that the attribution was made up entirely, as there is no print record of the quote — or any saying linking Einstein to the concept of compound interest — prior to that.

An investigation into the quote’s origins unearthed two very similar statements that may provide the ultimate inspiration for the eventual saying that became linked with Einstein’s name. In 1916, a newspaper advertisement in California described compound interest as “the greatest invention the world has ever produced.” A little bit later, in 1925, the phrase “the eighth wonder of the world is compound interest” was used by a Cleveland savings and loan company. It is unknown what sort of intersection of:

  • fabrication,
  • marketing by financial firms looking for investment,
  • and antisemitic thoughts (about the link between Einstein, Jews, and banks),

played a role in conferring an Einsteinian attribution to the actual quote itself.

The math of compound interest

When most of us think of growth, we think of what’s known as linear growth: where things grow by a given amount over a given interval. If you have a child and the child grows by 7.6 centimeters (3 inches) per year, then a baby who’s initially born at 51 centimeters (20 inches) will, after 17 years, have grown to a height of 180 centimeters (5 feet 11 inches). In linear growth, the amount that you gain does not depend on the amount that you already have. Instead, the growth is by a fixed amount over a given time. Financially, it would be like getting $100 every year on your birthday: after 17 years, you would have $1700.

On the other hand, compound interest accumulates based on the base amount that you already have. If you accumulate interest at a 4% rate annually, then if you start with $100, how much will you have after 17 years? You might think — and this is incorrect, linear thinking — that you should just multiply that 4% by 17 years, giving you 68%, growing your $100 to $168. But the way compound interest works is different.

  • For the first year, you earn 4% interest on $100, giving you $104.
  • For the second year, you earn 4% interest on $104, giving you $108.16.
  • For the third year, you earn 4% interest on $108.16, giving you $112.49.
  • For the fourth year, you earn 4% interest on $112.49, giving you $116.99.

And so on. Note that for each year beyond the first, you don’t just gain $4 a year (the 4% of the initial $100), but more than $4, as you get 4% interest on the full amount of your balance. By the time a full 17 years have elapsed, your initial $100 will have grown to $194.79: a significant increase over the $168 you’d expect with linear growth.

There are three factors that matter when it comes to compound interest.

  1. The first is simple: the rate of growth, known as the interest rate. If we took that same analysis — starting with $100 and growing it for 17 years — but upped the interest rate to 5%, 7%, or 9%, that initial investment would instead have grown to $229.20, $315.88, or $432.76, respectively after those 17 years elapsed.
  2. The second is also simple: the duration of time of the investment. If we go back to that original 4% interest rate, but consider longer-term investments, we can see how continued growth helps increase the amount that you gain. If you wait 30 years, 50 years, or (generationally) 250 years, your initial $100 would grow to $324.34, $710.67, or $1,812,737.11, respectively, at that same 4% rate. Time makes an enormous difference when it comes to compound interest, especially over the long run.
  3. The third is a little more complicated: how often the interest is compounded. In the prior examples, we compounded the interest annually: we calculated the interest based on how much we had as the principal amount at the start of the year, and then added the interest to the balance at the end of the year, where it becomes part of the new principal. After 17 years, if we compounded the interest quarterly, monthly, or daily, then instead of $194.79, we’d have $196.72, $197.16, or $197.38.

All three of these factors matter for the same underlying reason: interest gives you growth, and the amount of growth you get is determined by both the interest rate and the principal amount. When you grow the principal, you get interest not just on the original balance, but on the “amount of growth” too, and this accumulates over time.

Growing wealth from an investment

If you want to grow wealth via compound interest, the key is to maximize the value of your principal balance for as long as you can: during the maximal interest-earning times. In most instances, this means your best strategy is as follows.

  • Make the largest initial investment that you can. This, of course, is only doable with any starting assets that you have, as well as your “extra” income: your income minus taxes minus necessities. The more of an up-front investment you make, the more interest you earn right at the beginning of your investment: interest that keeps on earning more interest as time goes on.
  • Add to your principal balance when you can. Rather than just starting with an initial investment and earning interest on that, the more you continue to add to your investment, the more additional income you generate. Again: the earlier the better.
  • Go after the highest interest rate that you can. In general, not everyone gets the same interest rate for their investment: people who have more to invest get higher interest rates on their investments. Try to achieve the highest percentage that you can.
  • And maximize the frequency at which your interest is compounded. Continuously is the best, followed by daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, semiannually, and annually.

The idea is that the more you invest, the more your investments earn for you. Then, those earnings get reinvested, and that makes it possible for you to grow wealth. Of course, this method is only accessible to people who both are on the positive side of the balance ledger, and whose incomes are greater than their tax burdens plus their expenses.

Inflation: applying the same concept to prices

The flipside of compound interest, which grows your wealth, is inflation: the “compound interest” of the cost of goods. In the United States, they call this the CPI: Consumer Price Index, which is tracked monthly: an annual rate scaled by month-over-month cost increases (or decreases) of a variety of goods.

It’s a simple concept: if you earn a certain amount of (after-tax) income, that’s the amount you have available to spend on everything else. Since the inflation rate is calculated monthly, it’s straightforward to cumulatively calculate how much prices have gone up since a certain time period began: by calculating the monthly rate of inflation and then “compounding” the cost-of-living (or the prices of goods) with each new month that elapses.

If you look at the data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, you’ll find that deflation — or periods where things actually get less expensive — happened only in one year out of this entire century: during the financial crisis year (and the year of the Great Recession) of 2009. If you want to get things right, you’ll remember not just to look at the annual inflation rate, but rather to look at the monthly rate and compound the cost-of-living with each month that passes.

An example of the affordability crisis: Inflation in the United States in the 2020s

Let’s take a simple starting point as an illustration: how much money it requires, at a later time, to buy goods that would have cost $100 on January 1, 2020.

  • On January 1, 2021, you would have needed $101.24.
  • On January 1, 2022, you would have needed $106.10.
  • On January 1, 2023, you would have needed $114.93.
  • On January 1, 2024, you would have needed $119.77.
  • On January 1, 2025, you would have needed $123.36.
  • On January 1, 2026, you would have needed $126.75.
  • And on October 1, 2026, which is the most current data that’s presently available, you would have needed $129.96.

Over the span of 6 years and 9 months, what used to cost you $100 to buy now requires $130 to purchase. That’s a net increase in prices of 30%, which means that $100 today has only the same amount of purchasing power that $77 had in January of 2020.

If you feel that things cost more than they used to, and that the same amount of money doesn’t go as far as it used to, that is not your imagination: that is a consequence of inflation. For a year-over-year inflationary rate, there’s a tremendous difference between what’s been happening here in the 2020s and what happened previously in the 2000s and the 2010s. The average (annual) inflationary rate for the 2000s was 2.56%. The average (annual) inflationary rate for the 2010s was 1.77%. But here in the 2020s (so far), the average (annual) inflationary rate is 3.85%, or more than double what it was during the prior decade. Things aren’t just getting more expensive; they’re getting more expensive and staying more expensive than at any other time this century.

The increased effect of overinflated necessities and stagnated wage increases

Not everything, of course, has increased equally in cost over time. While the average cost of goods has increased 30% from the start of January, 2020, to the present day, the cost of certain commodities has gone up by much, much greater amounts than that average. For example:

  • Lumber, which affects the cost of housing and construction, has increased by 34%.
  • Crude oil, which affects the cost of fuels, plastics, and road materials, has increased by 65.6%.
  • Gasoline, which affects both the consumer retail price of gas and also shipping and transportation costs of all materials, including food, has increased by 75%.
  • Beef, a vital food staple in the United States, has increased by 94%.
  • Copper, which affects the prices of electrical, plumbing, and electronics equipment, as well as the cost of cars (especially electric vehicles), is up an astounding 125%.
  • And coal, which affects the cost of electricity and household utility bills, is up 111%.

If you’re interested in buying a home, you can expect to pay over 50% more, today, than you would have paid for the same home at the start of 2020. If you’re looking at what your monthly mortgage payment would be for buying that home today, it’s approximately double what it would have been at the start of 2020, as elevated interest rates combined with the extra expense of the house hit homebuyers with a double-whammy.

Wages have gone up in that time as well, but have not kept pace with the level of inflation that we’ve seen. Nominal wage earning growth from early 2020 is at 21%, the median earnings growth is up 23%, and the federal minimum wage has not increased at all: it has grown by 0%.

Meanwhile, the average cost of goods is up 30% over that same interval, and the cost of many necessities is up by greater amounts than that. Health insurance costs, for example, have risen by 5-7% per year from 2020 until today, far outpacing not only wage increases but also inflation.

If you want to keep pace with inflation, then that means your wages should be increasing not by a certain amount each year (or month, or whatever time period is chosen), but by the necessary percentage to keep pace with the cost of living. From January 2020 to the present day, the average cost of consumer goods has gone up by 30%. Can you say the same about your wages?

Although it’s still often attributed to Einstein, there is no record of him ever stating that, “Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn’t, pays it.” However, whether you understand or earn compound interest or not, everyone pays the cost of inflation: the compounding, rising prices of consumer goods and commodities. You pay it everywhere you go, from the gas pump to the grocery store to your health insurer, and you pay it unevenly: where your dollar only has 77% of the purchasing power it had at the start of 2020.

If you were struggling to make ends meet back in 2020, there’s an excellent chance that — if you’re like most American workers — you’re falling further behind now than you were back then. Inflation is compound interest for the cost of goods and commodities, and it’s something that everyone who makes purchases must reckon with. Understanding inflation is the key to understanding the affordability crisis, and it explains how the cost of living has gotten so high. The specifics that you face will vary from country-to-country, but affordability is a concern around the world, and understanding the two sides of compound interest is the key to solving this problem.

item.title: Mapping the brain won’t unlock all its secrets. That’s a good thing.
item.description:
There’s a quote attributed to New Zealand physicist Ernest Rutherford that goes something like this: “All science is either physics or stamp collecting.” In other words, some scientists perform experiments to explain how things work, while others don’t test specific hypotheses but instead observe the natural world and take note of what they find. The latter may seem inferior, but don’t underestimate the influence of observational science; after all, biology’s greatest stamp collector was probably Charles Darwin, who planted the seeds of his theory of evolution by natural selection in his detailed field journal published in 1839: The Voyage of the Beagle.  

In neuroscience, two types of stamp collections — wiring diagrams, or connectomes, and parts lists, or cell type atlases — are a major focus of time, effort, and financial investment. For example, the adult Drosophila connectome, published on a website called FlyWire.ai, is freely available for anyone to peruse. Upon its announcement, neuroscientist Sebastian Seung proclaimed in the New York Times that “mind uploading” had hit the mainstream.

The entire connectome, minimized to fit my computer screen, looks a bit like the tangled mess I pull out of my hairbrush every morning, except that each strand is color-coded to ease tracing its long, thin processes throughout the structure. Apparently, at least according to Seung, I’m staring at an uploaded mind. But what does it actually tell me? 

One is immediately struck by the sheer number of neurons and connections. It’s humbling, given that when I started as a student of neuroscience, I would blindly record from spiking neurons, one by one. It felt like trying to understand a whole planet full of people by speaking to one random person at a time. 

The connectome is a resource, but in and of itself it is not a specific answer to a specific question. Though it took an enormous amount of time, effort, and money to generate it, it’s not necessarily clear what breakthroughs will come of it and what those discoveries will mean for either basic science or human health. But does this matter? 

Until recently, the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans was the only organism for which a complete or near-complete connectome existed. Each of its 302 neurons is labeled, studied, and identified. 

The first draft of the C. elegans connectome was published by South African biologist Sydney Brenner and colleagues in 1986. Brenner, who started studying the species in the mid-1970s and championed it as a model, received a Nobel Prize in 2002 for his work in the role of genetics in its organ development. Fittingly, his Nobel lecture was titled “Nature’s Gift to Science” — an homage to the tiny worm and the value of selecting the appropriate model organism. 

Like other model organisms, C. elegans offers many practical benefits to a lab beyond its 302-neuron nervous system. It is one of the smallest and simplest organisms that is nevertheless multicellular (the fruit fly’s body, for example, comprises over half a million cells, while C. elegans has about 1,000 in total), and it is easy to maintain in bulk populations. Like other roundworms, C. elegans does not have blood or a respiratory system. It does, however, have an intestine and well-studied muscular structure. It is small — about one millimeter in length as an adult — and a large number of individuals can be kept in a single petri dish lined with agar, a jellylike substance commonly used in the lab to grow bacteria. The worms are remarkably sturdy creatures and can be purchased and stored easily in the freezer until they are thawed for use in experiments. They are particularly useful for research into the roles of genes in development, since their small number of cells are easy to track over their lifespans. On that last point, aging is a big topic of research in the species, as its lifespan of about two weeks is conveniently short. 

C. elegans is also one of the simplest and smallest organisms that nevertheless has a nervous system and exhibits complex behaviors such as thermotaxis (movement toward temperature cues), chemotaxis (movement toward chemical cues), and mating, among others. It is the most primitive organism known to exhibit a lethargic state comparable to sleep, and when exposed to nicotine, it exhibits some of the classic features of addiction, like withdrawal. 

The C. elegans connectome was generated using painstaking anatomical methods — essentially, slicing the microscopic worm into thin sections and imaging its cells using a powerful, high-resolution technique for preserved tissue called electron microscopy. More complete versions or variations of the worm’s connectome were published in the decades after Brenner’s initial version.

But it’s important to note here, in a truth at once frustrating and humbling, that neuroscientists still don’t fully understand how the C. elegans nervous system works despite having had a complete wiring diagram of it for decades. One of the major reasons for this is that the living nervous system, even in a worm, can behave differently — more dynamically and flexibly — than its static wiring diagram would suggest. To be fair, FlyWire gives us a lot of additional insight beyond showing connections. The Drosophila connectome it shows is not just a static map but a highly interactive and searchable database that scientists can use to quickly glean almost everything there is to know about their neuron, or brain region, of interest. We can compare the connectomes from male and female individuals, as well as from an adult brain and a larval brain, to understand how different cell types and connectivity patterns emerge throughout development or support sex-specific behaviors. 

But if there’s anything we’ve learned from connectome projects thus far, it’s that stamp collections of the brain’s cells, chemicals, and connections, as comprehensive as they are, raise far more questions than answers. 

Take, for example, the work of neuroscientist Eve Marder from Brandeis University. Marder spent years researching the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (STG) — a small circuit of about 30 neurons that generates rhythmic movements in a crustacean’s digestive system in response to food, in order to move it along the digestive tract and break it down. Her work, dating back to the 1990s, shows that even with a relatively simple circuit that produces a well-defined behavior, understanding the role of each neuron and each connection is anything but straightforward. 

One thing I’ve learned as a scientist, however, is that stamp collections like the connectome are worthy for precisely these reasons: They don’t give us the answers, but they help us to ask the right questions.

One major reason for this is that even in small circuits, neurons are highly interconnected in complex ways. For example, though a connectome can show synaptic connections between two neurons, scientists also need to know what type of connection it is: Neurons can exchange either chemical or electrical signals across synapses, and in some cases two neurons can share both types of connections. Neurons also can inhibit each other or be connected both directly and indirectly via other neurons, making their ultimate behavior in the circuit very hard to predict. Circuits that govern two different behaviors —  in the case of the lobster STG, two different digestive movements — are not neatly segregated. A neuron’s role therefore can’t be neatly categorized by which circuit or behavior it participates in. Finally, environmental conditions like temperature can impact the timing at which neurons fire and thus the downstream consequences of their activity. All of this suggests that though we can see wiring patterns in a connectome, we can’t necessarily tell which connections are important and under what conditions. 

One thing I’ve learned as a scientist, however, is that stamp collections like the connectome are worthy for precisely these reasons: They don’t give us the answers, but they help us to ask the right questions. According to longtime C. elegans researcher Cornelia Bargmann of Columbia University, who studies how the worm’s sense of smell drives complex feeding behaviors, “Every time we do an experiment, we look at those wiring diagrams and use them as a starting point for generating hypotheses.” Given the complexity of the brain, generating testable, well-reasoned hypotheses is often the hardest step. 

This is a point that is not often argued to policymakers and the public in defense of stamp collecting journeys in science, which often require huge investments of money, time, and effort. When I look at the Drosophila connectome and feel that I’ve never been farther away from understanding the brain, that is exactly how I’m supposed to feel. It means I’m on the right track. Because our biggest challenge in neuroscience, if not science in general, is to find out what we don’t know.

item.title: How your brain’s hemispheres actually work
item.description:
Neuropsychiatrist Iain McGilchrist has spent over three decades studying how the brain’s two hemispheres shape consciousness, and says almost everything we think we know about them is wrong. The “logical left, creative right” story that took hold in the 1980s and ’90s was never accurate. McGilchrist traces this back to a basic survival problem — how to eat without being eaten — and argues the right hemisphere’s mode of understanding, grounded in context and nuance, gets us closer to reality than the left’s ever can.
